strengths: The dual-branch architecture is intuitively motivated: Fourier processing supplies global interactions while the convolutional path retains spatially local, nonstationary structure.

DRIFT-Net consistently improves final-time relative L1 error over SCOT on the reported benchmarks, with particularly large gains on NS-PwC, while also reporting fewer parameters and higher throughput.
Component ablations cover low-frequency mixing, radial gating, and the frequency-weighted loss; the accompanying bandwise error analysis is relevant to the proposed mechanism.
The paper is generally well organized and explicitly acknowledges limitations involving hand-tuned spectral cutoffs, FFT overhead, two-dimensional experiments, and regular domains.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Low-frequency Fourier mixing, parallel spectral/spatial processing, additive fusion, radial frequency weighting, and frequency-weighted losses are individually established ideas; the paper does not clearly distinguish its construction from closely related hybrid Fourier-convolutional operators.

The central stability claims are not technically established. The spectral mixer is explicitly unconstrained, so convex gating does not make the mapping non-expansive relative to its input. The spatial branch and residual addition can further amplify perturbations, and an input-dependent gate contributes an omitted derivative term. The network-level result merely assumes that every DRIFT block has a smaller norm than every Swin block, without verifying this condition for the trained models.

The Sobolev defect theorem appears incorrect or insufficiently justified. With Lambda=(I-Delta)^(s/2), the stated loss already directly controls the L2 error, while the claimed dependence increases with the loss coefficient lambda rather than decreasing; the unusual exponent is unsupported by the proof sketch.

Experimental reporting is inadequate for reliable comparison: there are no uncertainty estimates, repeated seeds, test-set sizes, or statistical tests. Some improvements are modest enough that run-to-run variability could affect the conclusions.

Dataset and training details needed for reproduction are missing, including grid resolutions, temporal step sizes and horizons for several tasks, train/validation/test counts, physical parameters of the new Kolmogorov variants, optimizer values, model widths, spectral cutoffs, gate settings, and loss coefficients. The advertised code link is blank.

Baseline coverage is narrow. Comparisons are largely limited to SCOT and FNO, despite relevant convolutional, hybrid spectral-spatial, autoregressive-stability, and modern neural-operator baselines. FNO is omitted entirely on the two long-horizon datasets, and capacity is not matched across models.

The paper introduces an inference-only outer-band taper in the appendix without clearly stating whether it was used in reported results or ablating its effect. This creates ambiguity about the evaluated method.

The efficiency report is not sufficiently auditable: latency, memory use, hardware, batch size, resolution, and precision are not numerically specified, and the text confusingly says identical throughput numbers elsewhere correspond to a different resolution and precision configuration.

The empirical scope is restricted to two-dimensional Navier-Stokes-type problems on regular grids. This does not substantiate the broader claims of a generic, reusable PDE operator or PDE foundation-model component.

The new long-horizon results have extremely large relative errors, while only small absolute improvements over SCOT are obtained. No qualitative or physically meaningful diagnostics demonstrate that these rollouts remain useful.

strengths: The dual-branch architecture is intuitively motivated: global Fourier-domain processing complements local convolutional processing, while additive fusion avoids channel-width inflation.
Under the reported matched training conditions, DRIFT-Net consistently improves final-time error over SCOT across the evaluated tasks, with especially large gains on NS-PwC.
The component ablations cover low-frequency mixing, radial gating, and the frequency-weighted loss, and the paper also reports parameter count, throughput, rollout curves, and bandwise errors.
The manuscript is generally readable and openly acknowledges limitations concerning hand-tuned frequency cutoffs, FFT overhead, and restriction to two-dimensional flows.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis contains serious errors. In Lemma A.1, restricting an FFT to a low-frequency subset does not generally multiply its worst-case operator norm by the square root of that subset's area; a signal can concentrate all its energy in that subset. Consequently, Proposition A.2 does not establish the claimed tighter cumulative bound.

Theorem B.1 is unsupported and appears incorrect: the stated defect bound increases with the loss weight lambda, whereas the assumed weighted-loss bound directly suggests inverse dependence on lambda. The proof sketch does not justify the unusual 1/(2+s) exponent or its optimization argument.

The claimed stability advantage is not established. The complex mixer is explicitly unconstrained, the input-dependent gate contributes an omitted derivative term, and the convolutional/linear norm constraints discussed in the appendix are not said to be used during training. Proposition A.2 merely assumes the desired comparison with unmeasured SCOT norms.

The fusion equation does not operate as described. Because the mixed low-frequency tensor and high-frequency residual have disjoint support, the gate mostly attenuates each region rather than smoothly blending two competing signals at a boundary. Moreover, non-expansiveness of this spectral term does not imply non-expansiveness after it is added to the image branch and residual connection.

The empirical evidence is too limited for the broad claims. Comparisons use only SCOT and FNO, omitting relevant convolutional, spectral, autoregressive, and long-rollout neural-operator baselines. FNO is absent entirely from the two T=100 experiments.

Results lack test-set sizes, multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Several improvements are modest, so single-run test means are insufficient to establish reliable superiority.

The metric reporting is ambiguous or alarming: relative errors are defined as ratios, yet long-horizon values reach 57–111 without being labeled as percentages. If literal, these correspond to extremely poor rollouts; if percentage-scaled, the metric definition and all tables are inconsistent.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The advertised code link is blank, while essential dataset parameters, resolutions, split sizes, rollout horizons for the main tasks, architecture widths/depths, mask and band settings, loss coefficients, and full optimization details are missing.
An optional inference-only spectral taper creates an unexplained train-test discrepancy, and the paper does not state whether it was enabled for the reported results or ablate its effect.

The throughput discussion refers to a second resolution/precision configuration but provides neither that configuration nor separate measurements. The only qualitative visualization is explicitly illustrative, contains an apparently constant channel, and offers little evidence about prediction quality.

The method primarily combines established ingredients—Fourier mixing, a convolutional U-Net, gated fusion, and a frequency-weighted loss—without a convincing analysis or comparison demonstrating substantial novelty over existing hybrid spectral-spatial operators.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: limiting error accumulation in autoregressive PDE rollouts while retaining computational efficiency. The global-spectral/local-convolutional decomposition is intuitive and potentially useful.
Reported results are consistently favorable across four POSEIDON tasks and two longer-horizon Kolmogorov-flow variants, including sizable improvements on NS-PwC and NS-Tracer-PwC.
The efficiency results are attractive: DRIFT-Net reportedly uses 17M versus 20M parameters and achieves 158 versus 118 prediction steps/s under matched conditions.

weaknesses: The theoretical analysis contains serious errors. Restricting a Fourier multiplier to a fraction sigma_LF of frequencies does not generally reduce its worst-case L2 operator norm by sqrt(sigma_LF), since an input may concentrate entirely in that band. Thus Lemma A.1 and the claimed tighter cumulative Lipschitz bound are unsupported. Moreover, the comparison with Swin is conditional on inequalities that are neither enforced nor measured.

Theorem B.1 is also questionable: from lambda_hf times the squared Sobolev norm being at most epsilon, the direct L2 bound scales as sqrt(epsilon/lambda_hf), whereas the stated expression has a positive power of lambda_hf. The argument also conflates teacher-forced prediction error with the rollout defect evaluated at model-generated states.

The supposedly learnable cutoff is implemented using a hard floor and array slicing, which are non-differentiable with respect to the cutoff parameters. The text alternately describes the mask as learnable and its cutoff as hand-tuned. In addition, the pseudocode's [:kx,:ky] slice does not clearly include both positive and negative low frequencies along the full FFT axis or explain preservation of the required symmetry.

The evaluation is insufficiently reproducible. Essential details—including spatial resolution, task-specific rollout horizons, dataset split sizes, physical parameters and generation protocol for the two new datasets, architecture widths/depths, spectral bands, loss coefficients, taper coefficient, and optimizer settings—are absent. The abstract's code-availability statement contains no URL.

All results appear to be single runs, with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance analysis. This is especially problematic for improvements as small as 7.2% and roughly 3% on one long-horizon dataset.

Baseline coverage is too narrow for a top-tier claim: only SCOT and FNO are evaluated, with FNO omitted on the two new datasets. Comparisons against CNO, U-NO/U-FNO, AFNO-style models, PDE-Refiner, and parameter-matched convolutional or spectral backbones are missing. A ConvNeXt-only baseline and controls that add the proposed loss to SCOT are needed to isolate the architectural contribution.

The paper frames the method in terms of PDE foundation models and reusable transfer, but evaluates only closely related two-dimensional Navier–Stokes problems. There is no cross-equation transfer, pretraining/fine-tuning study, resolution generalization, out-of-distribution test, irregular geometry, or comparison across broader PDE families.

The reported relative-L1 values are ambiguous: values such as 110.87 are presented under a dimensionless ratio definition rather than as percentages. If literal, they indicate extremely inaccurate rollouts; if percentages, the tables and metric definition need to state the scaling explicitly.

An inference-only outer-band taper is introduced in the appendix without a reported coefficient or ablation, creating an additional test-time intervention that may affect the main results. Other architectural details are similarly unclear, including the figure's unexplained 'Mixup' component and the absence of explicit U-Net skip connections in the pseudocode.

Overall, the promising empirical signal does not overcome the incorrect theoretical claims, limited comparisons, ambiguity in the core implementation, and substantial reproducibility gaps. These issues place the current submission below the top-tier acceptance threshold despite a potentially worthwhile underlying idea.

strengths: The dual-branch design is intuitive: global low-frequency processing is combined with a local ConvNeXt-style branch while avoiding channel expansion through additive fusion.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering seven PDE benchmarks from multiple equation families plus two 100-step Kolmogorov-flow evaluations.
The paper includes useful component ablations, frequency-band diagnostics, parameter/memory/runtime measurements, width scaling, and limited hyperparameter sensitivity experiments.
DRIFT-NET achieves substantial improvements on some tasks, particularly NS-PwC and NS-Tracer-PwC, while using fewer parameters and less memory than scOT.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis contains a serious error: restricting an input to a low-frequency subset does not generally multiply the induced L2 operator norm by the square root of that subset's area. Thus Lemma A.1 and the claimed tighter cumulative Lipschitz bound are not established.

The remaining stability results do not support the paper's central claims. The comparison proposition merely assumes that every DRIFT block has a smaller norm than every Swin block, without verifying this condition; the actual complex mixer is explicitly unconstrained, and the input-dependent gate introduces an omitted derivative term. A pointwise convex-combination bound also does not make the full block non-expansive because the mixer and subsequent spatial addition can amplify signals.

Theorem B.1 is problematic: its stated defect is defined as the difference between the rollout prediction and applying the model to that same prediction, which is identically zero for the described autoregressive rollout. The unusual epsilon exponent is also unsupported by the proof sketch; the Sobolev norm already directly controls the L2 norm.

The method is underspecified and internally inconsistent. The learnable cutoff is implemented using floor applied to a sigmoid-scaled parameter, which is nondifferentiable under ordinary backpropagation; the main text, appendix, and pseudocode give different descriptions of the gate inputs; and essential values such as base width, number of radial bands, cutoff initialization, and frequency-loss hyperparameters are absent.

Results appear to come from one fixed-seed run, with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Several claimed gains are very small—for example 0.87 to 0.86 on Poisson–Gauss, 12.34 to 12.15 on Wave–Gauss, and 4.65 to 4.32 on FNS-KF—so their reliability cannot be assessed.

The long-horizon evidence is limited to scOT and yields final relative errors around 57–111 in the paper's unexplained units. These very large errors suggest severely degraded rollouts, while the modest advantage over scOT does not by itself demonstrate stable or physically faithful dynamics.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently demonstrated. DRIFT-NET and the baselines differ in parameter count, baseline-specific tuning is largely absent, and the adapted PDE-Refiner description does not establish that its original training/refinement procedure was faithfully reproduced. Relevant modern hybrid spectral-local alternatives are also missing.

Reproducibility is weak despite the extensive appendix: the abstract says code is available but provides no URL, precise dataset-generation and model settings remain incomplete, target rollout times are not enumerated per task, and the cross-resolution experiment relies on unspecified interpolation procedures.

The novelty is moderate: FFT-based low-frequency mixing, convolutional local processing, gating, and frequency-weighted losses are established ideas. The paper does not provide sufficiently rigorous analysis or controlled comparisons to show that their particular combination constitutes a major architectural advance.

strengths: The dual-branch spectral/spatial architecture is intuitive and potentially useful: global Fourier processing complements a local ConvNeXt-style image branch.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering seven PDE benchmarks and two additional long-horizon Kolmogorov-flow settings.
The paper reports relevant efficiency measurements and component ablations; DRIFT-NET is consistently more accurate and efficient than scOT under the reported setup.
The manuscript clearly acknowledges limitations involving hand-selected frequency cutoffs, FFT overhead, two-dimensional experiments, and regular grids.
weaknesses: The main theoretical analysis is unsound or inapplicable. Restricting an operator to a low-frequency subset does not generally introduce the claimed sqrt(sigma_LF) factor in its worst-case L2 operator norm, since an input may concentrate all its energy in that subset. Consequently, Lemma A.1 and the network-level comparison built upon it are not established.

The stability argument assumes norm-controlled spectral, convolutional, and linear maps, but the actual spectral matrix is explicitly unconstrained and the paper does not report imposing the stated projections on the other layers. The comparison with Swin is only conditional on an unverified inequality, while input-dependent gates add derivative terms that the analysis omits. Thus the theory does not support the claimed rollout stability.

The proposed 'convex fusion' combines components with disjoint frequency support. It primarily attenuates low and high bands rather than blending competing estimates at each frequency. Its pointwise bound is therefore weak, and it does not make the complete block non-expansive after the spatial branch, addition, and residual connection. Claims about preventing ringing and energy amplification are overstated.

The learnable cutoff is not technically specified. The pseudocode applies sigmoid, floor, and hard slicing, through which ordinary gradients cannot train the cutoff. It also uses [:kx,:ky], whereas the mathematical definition uses |kx| and should include the wrapped negative-frequency rows of an rFFT. This discrepancy affects both correctness and reproducibility.

All reported results appear to come from a single fixed seed, with no standard deviations or statistical tests. Several gains are very small, such as 0.87 to 0.86 on Poisson-Gauss, 1.10 to 1.03 on Allen-Cahn, and 12.34 to 12.15 on Wave-Gauss, so the evidence does not establish reliable superiority.

Baseline comparison is incomplete for the strongest claims. Architectures use one shared optimizer configuration without architecture-specific tuning, the long-horizon study compares only against scOT, and there is no comparison to closely related hybrid spectral-spatial or modern neural-operator designs. The novelty over existing Fourier/local hybrid operators and frequency-weighted losses is limited.

The paper repeatedly motivates PDE foundation models, pretraining, transfer, and modular replacement of attention, but all experiments train separate models from scratch. There is no multi-task pretraining, transfer evaluation, or actual plug-in experiment demonstrating the claimed relevance to foundation models.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the base width, number of radial bands, cutoff initialization, frequency-loss coefficient and exponent, exact target horizons, and warm-up settings. The abstract says code is available but provides no repository. Some reported metric values also appear to be percentages despite the definition omitting a factor of 100.

The cross-resolution experiment uses unspecified interpolation between resolutions and has no baseline, so nearly identical errors do not demonstrate genuine discretization or mesh generalization. The qualitative visualization is also weak, with one channel appearing saturated and little interpretable distinction between methods.

strengths: DRIFT-Net presents a coherent spectral–spatial architecture that combines global low-frequency processing with a local ConvNeXt-style branch; additive fusion avoids channel inflation and yields practical efficiency gains.

The empirical study is reasonably broad, covering seven elliptic, parabolic, hyperbolic, and Navier–Stokes tasks plus two 100-step Kolmogorov-flow variants. DRIFT-Net obtains the best reported mean error on every main benchmark.

The efficiency results are attractive: compared with scOT, the full model uses 17M versus 20M parameters, reduces peak training memory from 17.25 GB to 10.87 GB, and improves throughput from 118 to 158 steps/s.

Component ablations, spectral error plots, learning-rate sensitivity tests, width scaling, sample-efficiency results, and cross-resolution evaluation provide useful supporting evidence. weaknesses: The theoretical stability analysis contains serious gaps. Restricting an operator to a low-frequency subset does not generally reduce its worst-case L2 operator norm by the square root of that subset's area, since an input can concentrate entirely in that band. Consequently, Lemma A.1 and the resulting network-level comparison are not established as stated. Proposition A.2 is also conditional on a norm inequality that is neither enforced nor measured.

The claimed non-expansiveness is substantially overstated. The complex low-frequency matrix is explicitly unconstrained, the input-dependent gate contributes an omitted derivative term, and subsequent addition to the image branch and outer residual can amplify the representation. Appendix A discusses spectral-norm constraints or detached gates, but the reported model apparently uses neither.

The Sobolev defect bound is insufficiently justified and appears dimensionally questionable: the stated bound increases with the loss coefficient lambda, whereas stronger weighting should tighten rather than loosen control. The proof sketch does not establish the claimed exponent. These issues weaken the paper's advertised theoretical support for rollout stability.

The evaluation reports only single-seed test means, without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several improvements over scOT are small—approximately 1–7% on multiple tasks—and may fall within run-to-run variation. The long-horizon turbulent result is similarly modest, while absolute final errors exceed 100%, indicating that both models have substantially drifted.

Novelty is moderate. Low-mode Fourier mixing, parallel spectral/local processing, frequency-dependent gating, U-shaped operator networks, and Fourier-weighted losses all have close precedents. The related-work discussion does not sharply distinguish the method from combinations of FNO/U-FNO, global-filter networks, localized neural operators, and existing spectral-loss techniques.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The abstract's code link is blank, and important details—including the actual base width, number of radial bands, mask initialization, frequency-loss coefficients, taper settings, and warm-up duration—are missing. There are also inconsistencies between the radial-gate definitions in Appendix C and Algorithm 1, and it is unclear whether the inference-only taper was used for reported results.

The claim that the block is architecture-agnostic and reusable in PDE foundation models is not directly tested: experiments train task-specific models from scratch in one backbone, with no pretraining, cross-task transfer, or integration into multiple host architectures. Baseline tuning is also limited by imposing one common optimization recipe rather than reporting architecture-specific competitive tuning.
